text: Manasbal Lake is the deepest freshwater lake in the Safapora area of Ganderbal district, Jammu and Kashmir, India, named after the sacred Manasarovar. It is surrounded by four villages: Jarokbal, Kondabal, Nesbal (on the north-eastern side), and Gratbal. The lake is known for its lotus blooms (Nelumbo nucifera) that appear along its periphery during July and August, enhancing the beauty of its clear waters. A Mughal garden, Jaroka Bagh (meaning bay window), built by Nur Jahan, overlooks the lake. It is a significant site for birdwatching as it serves as one of the largest natural spawning grounds for aquatic birds in Kashmir and is referred to as the "supreme gem of all Kashmir Lakes." The rootstocks of the lotus plant, which grow extensively in the lake, are harvested and consumed by local communities. The lake is accessible from Srinagar via a 30-kilometre (19 mi) road passing through Shadipora, Nasim, and Ganderbal, and also from Sonmarg via Ganderbal. It lies on the route to Wular Lake, the largest lake in Kashmir. Locals believe the lake is ancient, though exact dating remains undetermined. Near the northern shore are ruins of a 17th-century Mughal fort, Jharokha Bagh, historically used by caravans traveling from Punjab to Kashmir. The lake is bordered by the Baladar mountains to the east, a lacustrine, fluviatile, and loessic elevated plateau known as 'Karewa' to the north, and the Ahtung hills to the south, which are used for limestone extraction. Along the Jhelum River, Manasbal Lake belongs to the third series of high-altitude lakes of the Himalayas, situated at 1,585–1,600 m (5,200–5,249 ft), classified as valley lakes (including Dal, Anchar, and Manasbal), distinct from high-altitude wetlands (in the Pir Panjal ranges) and glaciated lakes (in the inner Himalayas at 3,000–4,000 m). A fissure runs east to west through the center of the lake. The catchment area, covering 10 km² (3.9 sq mi), has no major inlet channels and is primarily fed by precipitation and over 1,200 springs; water flows out to the Jhelum River via a regulated channel. The lake supports fishing, food and fodder plant harvesting, navigation, transportation, tourism, and recreation. Water quality parameters include recorded flora and fauna: zooplankton, benthos, and fish, with economically important species such as Cyprinus (an exotic species introduced in 1956) noted, though indigenous fish populations have declined due to environmental changes. Eutrophication has been confirmed, with Ceratophyllum demersum spreading, dense mono-specific weed stands forming, reduced species diversity, prolonged anoxic conditions, and accumulation of H₂S in deeper waters, along with pollution from the absence of wastewater treatment plants. The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), which surveyed the lake in 1997, identified the causes of its degradation, particularly the transformation of its banks into a stinking marsh. WWF recommended restoration measures, which were only implemented in 2007 with the establishment of the Wular-Manasbal Development Authority (WMDA) under the Government of Jammu and Kashmir. The WMDA initiated restoration efforts, with the chief executive officer stating that community participation was achieved after long discussions with locals, emphasizing that conservation is vital not only for tourism but also for livelihoods. A Shikara operator reported significant improvements in the lake’s condition. During restoration work, an ancient Hindu temple was discovered on the eastern shore, dating to 800–900 AD during the Avantivarman or Sankaravarman rule, constructed in local grey stone with a unique pyramid-shaped roof and floral motifs, serving as a new pilgrimage site for visitors to Amarnath and Kheer Bhawani temples. Other attractions include the Manasbal Temple, ruins of a terraced Mughal garden, and sculptured stones of Sufi shrines. The National Cadet Corps (NCC) began in Kashmir in 1965, but its training facility at Manasbal was abandoned in 1989 due to security issues. In September 2022, the Indian Navy revived NCC naval training at Manasbal, with 100 cadets—including girls from various colleges—participating in activities such as boat pulling, sailing, signaling, and ship modeling. The Manasbal Development Authority provided a suitable camping site and infrastructure. Previously, such training occurred in Nagrota and Mansar Lake. The lake offers pleasant weather in May and August, when water skiing is popular, supported by the Jammu & Kashmir Tourism Department (JKTD), which provides equipment and trained instructors. The lake’s surface sheen and size attract skiers, but concerns remain about the environmental impact of water skiing, as noise and turbulence could disrupt the lake’s tranquility and risk turning it into a second Dal Lake. There is ongoing debate about whether a more environmentally sensitive, sustainable tourism model would be better suited for preserving the lake’s peace and ecological integrity.
